title: Model-Informed Deep Q-Networks to Guide Infliximab Dosing in Pediatric Crohn's Disease

content.abstract_summary: Develops a model-informed Deep Q-Network (DQN) to automate and personalize infliximab dosing in pediatric Crohn's disease. The DQN is trained in a simulation environment using a population PK model and virtual pediatric patients over 80,000 episodes. Retrospectively validated against real clinical data from REFINE + APPDASH studies. First application of Q-learning to infliximab and first real-world validation of an RL-based precision dosing framework for biologics in pediatrics. From Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, NIH-funded.
key_findings: DQN achieves 92.9% target attainment probability (PTA) at Infusion 4 and 98.4% at Infusion 5 vs 27.8% and 22.4% with standard 5 mg/kg weight-based dosing — a 3-4× improvement in target attainment

High doses (11-20 mg/kg) selected in only 0.2% of virtual patients with decision-based reward function — the reward structure successfully penalizes unnecessary dose escalation, a clinically critical safety constraint
Standard 8-week dosing interval maintained for 66.8% of patients at Infusion 4 and 57.3% at Infusion 5 — RL learns clinically preferred dosing behaviors when embedded in the reward function

Retrospective real-world validation: patients whose actual doses aligned with DQN recommendations had trough concentrations significantly closer to target ranges (Spearman correlation at Infusions 4 and 5) — first real-world validation of RL dosing for a biologic

No correlation at Infusion 1 (baseline covariates only): DQN cannot outperform population predictions for initial dosing without concentration data — a fundamental PK uncertainty that RL cannot overcome without feedback

DQN converged after 80,000 training episodes using double DQN with dueling architecture and prioritized experience replay — standard deep RL components enable stable learning in continuous covariate space
limitations: PK model trained on only 78 pediatric patients (Xiong) — small training set limits generalizability of the underlying PK model driving the simulation environment
Limited PD biomarkers (no fecal calprotectin, clinical remission status) — DQN can only optimize PK exposure targets, not disease outcomes directly
Initial dosing (Infusion 1) limited by absence of concentration feedback — RL cannot improve over population-level predictions without any observed drug levels
Real-world validation is retrospective and associational, not prospective causal — DQN concordance correlates with target attainment partly because both reflect accurate PK model predictions

extracted_claims.text: This is the first study to apply Q-learning to infliximab therapy and to validate an RL-based precision dosing framework using clinical data.
Target attainment probabilities (PTAs) of 92.9% and 98.4% at Infusions 4 and 5, respectively, in 1000 virtual patients.
High doses (11-20 mg/kg) were selected in only 0.2% of cases.

numerical_findings.description: Target attainment probability (PTA) at Infusion 4: DQN vs standard 5 mg/kg
Target attainment probability (PTA) at Infusion 5: DQN vs standard 5 mg/kg

gaps_addressed: Fills M3.2 (deep RL for model-informed precision dosing) with a concrete biologic/immunology application — a different drug class (mAb vs the HDAC inhibitor givinostat and kinase inhibitor erdafitinib in the de_carlo papers)
First real-world retrospective validation of RL-based dosing (the de_carlo papers use only virtual populations) — directly relevant to the M3 question of translational readiness

The reward function design (penalizing high doses and extra clinic visits) illustrates how clinical constraints and safety preferences can be encoded in RL without changing the PK model — a practical contribution for the WG tutorial

provenance.notes: Found via PubMed search 'reinforcement learning drug dosing pharmacokinetics optimal' (PMID 41189499). PMC12816428 (open access). CPT 2025, 119(2):555-563. Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (Mizuno T = corresponding). NIH-funded (DK132408 from NIDDK). Crohn's and Colitis Foundation. The first ML/RL paper from a purely clinical translational team (not a methods group like U Pavia) — adds credibility for clinical adoption angle. The CCHMC clinical dashboards (RoadMAB platform) mentioned as integration target.
